lesson.title: The Top of the Chain: What Makes a Network Tier 1
lesson.summary: A tier 1 ISP is a network that reaches the entire internet without ever paying for transit, relying solely on settlement free peering with other tier 1 networks plus its own paying customers.
lesson.body:
Among the many autonomous systems that make up the internet's core, a small number occupy a distinct position, and it comes from a business relationship, not from a technical rule enforced by any protocol. A tier 1 network, sometimes called a tier 1 ISP, is a network that can reach every other routable network on the internet without ever paying anyone for transit. It achieves complete reachability entirely through settlement free peering with the other tier 1 networks, where each carries the other's traffic to its own customers at no charge, since the exchange of value runs both ways, plus the transit relationships in which its own customers pay it. No tier 1 network has to buy access to the rest of the internet from some larger network above it, because there is no larger network above it, it sits at the top of the chain described when looking at internet topology.

This is worth restating because it is easy to mistake for a technical or size based definition, and it is neither. Tier 1 status is defined entirely by the absence of a purchased transit relationship: an operator either has settlement free peering arrangements that, together, cover the whole internet, or it does not, in which case it is buying transit from someone, however large it otherwise is, and is not tier 1 by this definition. Peering agreements themselves are typically private, bilateral, and not publicly documented in complete detail, and which networks currently qualify as tier 1 has genuinely shifted over the internet's history, as mergers happen and peering relationships are added, changed, or occasionally broken off in disputes, so it is more useful to understand tier 1 status as a description of a network's peering position than as a fixed membership list.

The practical consequence for everyone downstream is that tier 1 networks form the backbone the rest of the internet ultimately depends on. A packet crossing between two customers of two different smaller providers on opposite sides of the world will frequently transit through one or more tier 1 networks along the way, even though neither endpoint has any direct relationship with those tier 1 networks at all, because those smaller providers themselves buy transit from, or peer through, larger networks that eventually connect into that settlement free tier 1 mesh.
